events.title: THE EXPEDITION BEGINS USING THE SECONDARY PASSAGE AS ITS MAIN LINE OF MARCH
events.body: The expedition leaves the temporary camp and begins using the secondary passage tested during the previous week as its principal line of movement. The route is easier than the steep face of the first difficult pass, but its usefulness still depends on careful inspection as the party advances beyond the ground already examined. The scribes compare the new day's terrain with the route register sealed at the end of the previous round. Because the country farther ahead remains unfamiliar, the expedition continues to record each verified section separately from what guides claim lies beyond it. The day's movement consumes additional provisions while extending the firsthand geographic record. By evening, the party has established another verified segment of the route without fixing a final destination for the journey.

events.title: TRAVELERS BRING AN ACCOUNT OF THE ROAD NETWORK TOWARD SPOLETIUM
events.body: A small group of travelers encountered near the route provides an account of roads and valleys that, in their telling, lead toward the wider country associated with Spoletium. Their testimony gives the expedition another regional reference, but none of the travelers can establish the exact position of Valerius's present camp. The scribes record their statements separately from the ground personally inspected by the expedition. The account is compared with the earlier geographic frame that also referenced Narnia, Interamna Nahars, Fulginium, and Iguvium as regional anchors rather than claimed destinations. The comparison produces a more coherent picture of the surrounding road system while preserving uncertainty about the expedition's exact location. The travelers depart without altering the expedition's chosen route.

events.title: A SUDDEN STORM INTERRUPTS THE AFTERNOON MARCH
events.body: A sudden storm reaches the expedition during the afternoon march and turns an already rough section of the passage into a short-lived hazard. The party halts long enough to secure the heavier loads and keep the animals from being driven onto unstable ground. The interruption costs additional provisions and forces the scribes to postpone the next stage of their route measurements until visibility improves. No casualties or permanent losses are recorded, and the expedition resumes movement once the worst of the weather has passed. The event gives the field record its first direct observation of how quickly the usable character of the route can change with weather. The passage remains serviceable, but the expedition now treats the exposed section with greater caution.

events.title: MARCELLUS'S REPLY REINFORCES THE SEPARATION OF OBSERVATION AND TESTIMONY
events.body: A reply from Marcus Claudius Marcellus reaches the documentary chain surrounding the expedition and acknowledges the distinction between firsthand observation and testimony in the field papers. Marcellus does not attempt to redirect the expedition or name a new destination. Instead, his response places value on preserving the uncertainties within the record rather than smoothing them away for the sake of a simpler account. The scribes add the reply to the same documentary packet that contains the earlier inquiry and the expedition's preliminary notes. This strengthens the institutional connection between Valerius's household archive and the Roman correspondents following the expedition. The route itself remains governed by field observation rather than by the correspondence.

events.title: THE ESTATE'S STORES ARE REBALANCED WHILE THE EXPEDITION REMAINS AWAY
events.body: At the estate, the stewards rebalance grain and fodder stores between the older acreage and the recently purchased tract while spring work continues. The adjustment is administrative rather than a new harvest or sale, and the property records remain unchanged at 7.75 square miles. Workers continue coordinating water and labor with the arrangements already established for nearby smallholders. The larger spring workload consumes another portion of the household's available supply resources. Agriculture is already recorded at its maximum value, so the continued cultivation produces no additional agricultural points. The revised store ledger gives the household a clearer account of what remains available while Valerius is away.

events.title: METELLUS CELER'S CHANNEL REQUESTS THE NEXT COPIED MAP SHEET
events.body: A further communication associated with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer requests a copied map sheet once the expedition has accumulated enough verified route material to make the copy useful. The request does not disclose a hidden order and does not require the field party to interrupt its movement. The scribes prepare to duplicate only the sections already supported by direct observation, leaving uncertain territory visibly unresolved in the working record. The request connects the expedition's practical work with the continuing Roman interest already established in the correspondence. No new payment, contract, or financial realization accompanies the message. The expedition therefore retains both its freedom of movement and its growing documentary obligation.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION REACHES A SAFER CAMPING GROUND AND PREPARES THE NEXT SURVEY
events.body: The expedition reaches a safer camping ground at the end of the week's movement and settles without claiming that the site is a known historical settlement. The route register is updated with the sections personally inspected during the week's march, while the travelers' descriptions remain marked as testimony. The field party has now moved beyond both the first difficult pass and the secondary passage while still preserving uncertainty about the country farther ahead. The scribes inventory the route evidence before darkness and prepare a fresh sheet for the next stage of exploration. The expedition remains active and has not begun a return journey to Rome. The week therefore closes with a longer tested route and a cleaner distinction between direct evidence and inherited geographic reports.
